items.title: AI Learns Through Continuous Data Conversations #DataScience #MachineLearning #AILearning
items.content_snippet: Building effective AI for data analytics isn't a one-and-done implementation. As Chris Merrick explains, the real magic happens when you build a continuous feedback loop between the system and the user. We explored the framework for scaling these capabilities: - Going Deeper: Continuously upgrading AI to handle increasingly complex data models and follow-up analysis questions. - Going Broader: Expanding the AI's reach into adjacent workflows to support broader engineering and business context. -

items.title: Amazon Neptune now supports tag-based access control for IAM

items.title: AWS Glue Data Quality now supports anomaly detection and writing results to the AWS Glue Data Catalog
items.content_snippet: AWS Glue Data Quality now supports anomaly detection for Catalog-based data quality evaluations and the ability to write evaluation results to AWS Glue Data Catalog (GDC) tables. These capabilities work across both ETL jobs and Catalog evaluations, giving you a consistent data quality experience regardless of workflow type. With anomaly detection support for GDC, you can identify unexpected changes in data statistics such as sudden drops in distinct values or row count spikes in your GDC tables

items.title: AWS Glue Data Quality now supports distribution statistics for data profiling

Using this new Distribution Analyzer in the Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL), you can generate histograms for numeric columns and value distributions for categorical, date, and boolean columns. items.title: AI Agents for Performance: Ship Faster, Pay Less — Rajat Shah, Netflix
items.content_snippet: An inefficient quadratic-time pattern was hiding inside a tensor merge method on a live Netflix service, quietly wasting CPU on every request - nothing in a code review caught it, but it stood out clearly in a call stack. That's usually how this kind of waste gets missed - the normal process of catching it (profiling, reading a flamegraph, tracing it through the codebase, writing a fix, validating it) takes long enough that inefficiencies sit in production for months before anyone looks at them.
